title: Anatomy of the Skin
displayTitle: EMLAAnatomy of the Skin

body:
The skin covers the entire external surface of the human body. The skin might not be thought of as an organ, but all the tissue and structures within the skin work together to perform several functions. The skin and its accessory structures are referred to as the integumentary system, the main function of which is protection of the body.

The skin is the primary site for interaction between the body and the external environment. It serves as a protective barrier that prevents the internal tissues from exposure to trauma, ultraviolet radiation, temperature extremes, toxins and bacteria. The skin is also an important component of the sensory system, the immune system, thermoregulation and regulation of fluid loss.

The skin, or integument is made up of three mutually dependent layers, the epidermis and dermis, which rests on an underlying fatty subcutaneous layer (hypodermis).

_items.body: The skin is a dynamic organ and is continuously undergoing changes throughout life. The outer layers are shed, and are replaced by newer, inner layers. Skin also varies in thickness across various locations on the body, with the thickest being on the palms and soles of the feet and the thinnest skin on the eyelids and in the postauricular region. Note that it is generally the dermis which varies in thickness, as the epidermis has a relatively constant thickness across the body.

Males tend to have thicker skin than females, and children have relatively thin skin that will thicken with age. However, as people reach 40 to 50 years of age, skin starts to thin. This is a natural process and is due to loss of elastin fibres, epithelial appendages, and underlying tissue.

title: Layers of the Skin
body:
The skin is made up of three layers:
  • Epidermis
  • Dermis
  • Subcutaneous fat layer (hypodermis)
Each layer has specific functions.

title: Epidermis
body:
The epidermis is the thin, tough outer layer of the skin.

The epidermis is a stratified, squamous epithelium layer and is mostly made up of two types of cells – keratinocytes and dendritic cells. Keratinocytes make up many of the cells in the epidermis. There are also other cells found within the epidermis and include melanocytes, Langerhans cells and Merkel cells. These cells make up a smaller proportion of the skin.

The epidermis is made up of four or five layers, depending on the location in the body. The layers are differentiated by the keratinocyte morphology and position as they change through the layers from keratinocytes to horny cells.

The layers of the skin, from deepest to most superficial are:
  • Stratum basale
  • Stratum spinosum
  • Stratum granulosum
  • Stratum corneum
instruction: Select the picture below to read more.

_items.backBody: These four layers make most of the “thin” epidermis found across the body. The “thick” epidermis is made up of 5 layers and is found on the soles of the feet and palms of the hands. This fifth layer is the stratum lucidum, which is found between the stratum granulosum and the stratum corneum.

body: The epidermis is continually renewing these layers as new cells from the stratum basale move up towards the surface. These cells, the keratinocytes, change as they move through the layers until they reach the stratum corneum. These keratinocytes are dead and are sloughed off, to be replaced by newer keratinocytes from deeper layers.
instruction: Select Continue to open the remaining text.

_next.ariaLabel: Select here to move to the next.

_items.body: The epidermis has no blood vessels, i.e., avascular, and is dependent on the dermis to supply nutrients and waste removal through the dermoepidermal junction.
The stratum corneum is relatively waterproof and provides protection to the underlying layers from infiltration by bacteria, viruses or foreign substances.
The epidermis also protects the internal organs, muscles, nerves and blood vessels from trauma.

title: Epidermal cells
instruction: Select the tabs below to learn more.

_items.body:
A keratinocyte is a cell that manufactures and stores keratin. Keratin is an intracellular, fibrous protein that gives hair, nails and skin their hardness and water-resistant properties. At least 80% of the epidermis is derived from keratinocytes. As the cells move from the basal layer to the surface, they undergo differentiation through a process known as keratinisation.

As the cells move from the basal layer to the stratum corneum they lose their organelles, and the contents of the cells consolidate to form horny cells or corneocytes. These cells are in effect dead as they have no nucleus and are sloughed away from the surface of the skin.

Melanocytes are dendritic, pigment producing cells and are found predominantly in the basal layer. Melanocytes are responsible for the production of melanin, the substance with provides pigmentation to the skin and protects the skin from harmful effects of ultraviolet (UV) radiation by absorbing the radiant energy from the sun. Melanocytes are also found in the hair follicles, the retina, the uveal tract and leptomeninges.

Langerhans cells originate from bone marrow and are found in the basal, spinosum and granulosum strata. Langerhans cells are specialised dendritic cells, and do not form any junctions with adjacent cells. These cells make up 2 to 8% of the epidermal cells. Langerhans cells play a role in immunity by serving as antigen-presenting cells.

Merkel cells are oval-shaped, slow adapting mechanoreceptors. Merkel cells are found in areas that are highly sensitive to tough, such as the lips, digits, nail beds and on genitalia to name a few.

These cells require only slight deformation in the adjoining keratinocytes to produce a stimulus in the Merkel cells sufficient to cause a signal to be generated and sent to the brain. Merkel cells are specialised cells for the stimulation of light touch.

body: As mentioned, the epidermis has 4 or 5 layers, depending on the type of skin. Each layer is made up of different cells and provides a specific function.

title: Epidermal layers
instruction: Select the headings to learn more.
_comment: setCompletionOn = inview | allItems

_items.title: Stratum Basale
_items.body:
• Basal layer – deepest layer.
  • Connects epidermis to basal lamina.
  • Collagen fibres bind layer to dermis.
  • Single layer of basal cells:
    • Cuboidal-shaped stem cells.
    • Precursors for keratinocytes.
  • All keratinocytes produced from this layer.
  • New cells produced, push older cells upwards to upper epidermal layers.
  • Contains papillae – finger-like projections:
    • Increase strength of connection between epidermis and dermis.
    • The more papillae present the stronger the connection.
  • Also contains Merkel cells and melanocytes.

_items.title: Stratum Spinosum
_items.body:
• Made up of 8 – 10 layers of keratinocytes.
  • Spiny appearance because of cell processes.
  • Desmosomes interlock and strengthen bond between cells.
  • Keratinocytes begin to synthesize keratin and release glycolipid that repel water.
  • Helps prevent water loss and makes skin waterproof.
  • Also contains Langerhans cells.

_items.title: Stratum Granulosum
_items.body:
• Made up of 3 to 5 layers of keratinocytes.
  • Granular appearance because keratinocytes have changed shape:
    • Flattened and thicker cell membranes.
  • Produces more keratin.
  • Produces keratohyalin:
    • Accumulate as lamellar granules within the cells.
  • As keratinocytes move upwards through the layer, nuclei and other organelles disintegrate as cells die.
  • Leave behind keratin, keratohyalin and cell membranes:
    • Make up the stratum lucidum, stratum corneum and certain accessory structures such as hair and nails.

_items.title: Stratum Lucidum
_items.body:
• Only found in thicker epidermal skin.
  • Smooth, almost transparent layer.
  • Made up of dead, flattened keratinocytes.
  • Densely packed with protein called eleidein:
    • Protein rich in lipids.
    • Derived from keratohyalin.
  • Provides waterproof barrier to skin.

_items.title: Stratum Corneum
_items.body:
• Most superficial layer, exposed to the environment.
  • 15 to 30 layers of cells.
  • Increased keratinisation (called cornification).
  • Dry, dead layer that prevents penetration by foreign particles and microbes.
  • Prevents dehydration of underlying tissues.
  • Provides protection from mechanical damage.
  • It is sloughed off and replaced regularly:
    • Entire layer is replaced during a 4-week period.

title: Dermis
body: The layer beneath the epidermis is the dermis. This layer is an integrated system of fibrous and elastic tissues, the majority being collagen and the remainder a small but important component of elastin. This layer gives skin its flexibility and strength.
instruction: Select the pictures below to read more.

_items.backBody:
Collagen

Collagen is a fibrous, protein that has at least 15 genetically different variations in the human skin. Collagen is a major structural component throughout the body and can be found in ligaments, tendons, the lining of bones and the dermis. It is a stress resistant material, which allows for the skin to be pliable. Collagen fibres are in a constant state of flux, meaning that the fibres are continuously degraded and replaced by new fibres. Collagen represents 70% of the skin’s dry weight.

Elastin

Elastin fibres are made up from elastin and protein filaments. These fibres maintain the elasticity of the skin but are not stress resistant, so therefore do not protect the skin from tearing or being deformed.

body: Both collagen and elastin are produced by fibroblasts, the major cell found in the dermis.

title: Dermis
instruction: Select the button below until you have opened all the points.

_items.body: The dermis also contains blood vessels, nerve endings, fibroblasts, sebaceous glands, sweat glands and hair follicles.

The dermis makes up the bulk of the skin and is responsible for elasticity, pliability, and tensile strength of the skin. It also provides protection from mechanical injury, thermal regulation, binds water and plays a role in sensory perception. Through interacting with the epidermis, the dermis maintains both layers of the skin.

The dermis is made up of two layers of connective tissue that are composed of an integrated mesh of collagen and elastin:
  • Papillary layer.
  • Reticular layer.

title: Fibroblasts
body: Fibroblasts are the main type of cell within the dermis. These cells produce and secrete procollagen and elastin fibres. Fibroblasts are the least specialised of the connective tissue cells and can differentiate into different cells within the extracellular matrix.
instruction: Select Continue to open the remaining text.

_next.ariaLabel: Select here to move to the next.

_items.body: Procollagen is the precursor to collagen. Proteolytic enzymes cleave the procollagen into collagen that aggregates and becomes cross-linked. These cross-linked fibres are what provide the tensile strength and tear-resistance observed with collagen.

Collagen has various structural forms, but the form most found in the dermis is collagen Type I (85%).  Collagen type III makes up the remaining 15%. Elastin fibres make up less than 1% of the weight of the dermis.

title: Mast Cells
body: Mast cells are specialised secretory cells derived from bone marrow and are found in connective tissue throughout the body. They are also found in subcutaneous fat. Mast cells play a role in allergic response and inflammation.

title: Papillary Layer
instruction: Drag the circle along the horizontal line to reveal more information.

_items.title: Item 1
_items.body: This layer is the first layer of the dermis and is made of loose, areolar connective tissue. The collagen and elastin fibres form a loose mesh.

_items.title: Item 2
_items.body: This layer projects into the stratum basale of the epidermis as dermal papillae. This structure helps to strengthen the connection between the two layers.

_items.title: Item 3
_items.body: The papillary layer contains fibroblasts, a small number of adipocytes and many small blood vessels.

_items.title: Item 4
_items.body: There are also phagocytes which play a role in the defence of the body from invasion by pathogens that have entered the skin.

_items.title: Item 5
_items.body: Lymphatic capillaries, nerve fibres and touch receptors called Meissner corpuscles are also found in this layer of the dermis.

title: Reticular Layer
body: The layer beneath the papillary layer is the reticular layer. This is a thicker layer made up of dense, irregular connective tissue. This layer is highly vascularised, meaning there are many blood vessels, particularly larger ones. There is also a rich sensory and sympathetic nerve supply.

instruction: Select the button below until you have opened all the points.

_next.ariaLabel: Select here to move to the next.

_items.body: The tight mesh of coarse collagen fibre bundles and interlaced elastin fibres provides the structure and strength to the layer.
The elastin allows the skin to move.
Strands of collagen extend from the reticular layer into the hypodermis.
This layer also contains fibroblasts, mast cells, nerve endings, lymphatic and epidermal appendages.
Surrounding all components of the dermis is a gel-like substance that is composed of mucopolysaccharides, predominantly hyaluronic acid, chondroitin sulphates and glycoproteins.

body:
The dermoepidermal, or dermal-epidermal junction is the basement membrane that adheres the epidermis to the dermis. Basal keratinocytes make up most cells within the junction with a smaller number of dermal fibroblasts. This membrane allows for the exchange of cells and fluids between the 2 layers.

The junction is composed of 2 layers:
  • Lamina lucida
  • Lamina densa

title: Dermo-epidermal Junction
instruction: Select the pictures below to reveal more information.

_items.backBody: The lamina lucida is thinner and lies beneath the basal layer of epidermal keratinocytes. The lamina densa is thicker and touches the underlying dermis. The plasma membranes of the basal cells are connected to the lamina lucida by rivet-like hemi-desmosomes. These structures distribute the tensile strength throughout the epidermis.

The dermal papillae extend from the epidermis into the dermis and contain a plexus of capillaries and lymphatic vessels that lie perpendicular to the skin surface. The irregular junction increases the surface area over which oxygen, nutrients and waste products can be exchanged between the epidermis, which is avascular, and the dermis.

body: Besides providing supporting the epidermis the dermoepidermal junctions has several other functions, including establishing cell polarity and direction of growth, directing organisation of the basal cytoskeleton, provides developmental signals and creating a semi-permeable barrier between the 2 layers.

The hypodermis, or subcutaneous fat layer, is the last layer of the skin. This layer joins the skin to the underlying fascia of the bones and muscles.

The hypodermis is composed of well-vascularised, loose, areolar connective tissue and adipose tissue. The lobules of fat are separated by fibrous septae made from large blood vessels and collagen.

Adipose tissue is made up of adipocytes, cells which store fat. This stored fat is a reserve of energy, insulates the body and protects the underlying structures.

title: Accessory Structures of the Skin
body: Sweat glands develop from epidermis projections that go into the dermis. These glands are known as merocrine glands because the secretions from these glands are excreted by exocytosis through a duct. This process does not affect the cells of the glands. There are 2 types of sweat glands, each of which secrete a slightly different substance.

title: Sweat Glands
instruction: Select the pictures below to reveal more information.

_items.backBody:
Eccrine Sweat Gland

Eccrine sweat glands are involved in thermoregulation. These glands produce hypotonic sweat and are found all over the body. Eccrine sweat glands are found in greater abundance on the soles of the feet, palms of the hands and the forehead. These are coiled glands that lie deep within the dermis, with a duct that rises into a pore on the skin surface.

Apocrine Sweat Gland

The apocrine sweat glands are primarily involved in the release of scent. These glands are normally associated with hair follicles in areas where there is a lot of hair, such as the armpits and genital areas. These sweat glands are larger than eccrine sweat glands and lie deeper in the dermis, possibly reaching into the hypodermis.

title: Sebaceous Glands
body: Sebaceous glands are a type of oil gland found all over the body, with the greatest number being on the scalp and face. Most sebaceous glands are associated with hair follicles.
instruction: Select the picture below until you have seen all the information.

_items.body: Sebaceous glands are responsible for lubrication and waterproofing of the skin and hair. Sebaceous glands produce and secrete sebum, a mixture of lipids, onto the skin’s surface where it naturally lubricates the dry and dead keratinised cells of the stratum corneum. This keeps the stratum corneum pliable.
Sebum also contains fatty acids, which have antibacterial properties thereby providing some protection from pathogens. The fatty acids are also responsible for the retention of water in the skin.

Sebaceous glands and the secretion of sebum is stimulated by hormones. Many of the hormones responsible for this secretion are only activated in puberty, so the glands are predominantly inactive during childhood.

title: Hair
body: Hair is a filament made from keratin that grows out of the epidermis. Hair is mostly made up of dead, keratinised cells. A hair is made up of several parts. The table below details the properties of the different components of hair.

Hair componentProperties
Hair follicleHair originates from follicle.
Hair shaft
  • Part of hair that is not anchored to the follicle.
  • Most of the shaft is exposed on skin’s surface.
Hair root
  • Remainder of hair.
  • Anchored in follicle.
  • Lies beneath surface of skin.
Hair bulb
  • End of hair root.
  • Located deep in dermis.
Hair matrixLayer of mitotically active basal cells.
Hair papilla
  • Surrounded by hair bulb.
  • Composed of connective tissue.
  • Contains blood capillaries and nerve endings from the dermis.
Hair has many functions including protection, thermoregulation, sensory input and communication.
instruction: Select Continue to open the remaining text.

_next.ariaLabel: Select here to move to the next.

_items.body: With regards to protection, the different areas of hair provide various forms of protection. For example, the hair on the scalp protects the underlying skin from UV radiation. The hairs within the ears and nose trap and remove dust particles and allergens that could possibly enter the body.

Thermoregulation is achieved through the “standing up” of the hairs. Each hair root is connected to a smooth muscle, known as the arrector pili. This muscle contracts in response to signals from the sympathetic nervous system. When the muscle contracts the external hair shaft stands up. This allows for a thin layer of air to be trapped against the skin which provides additional insulation.

The innervation of the hair root allows for sensory perception. Hair is very sensitive to air movement and other disturbances from the environment, which provides external sensory stimuli. This allows for the detection of harmful or bothersome substances on the skin surface.

title: Nails
body: The nails are located at the tips of the fingers and toes. The body of the nail is made up of densely packed dead keratinocytes. The epidermis has evolved to provide the specialised structures needed for nail growth.

title: Blood Supply
body:
The blood vessels that supply the skin are found in the dermal layer. This dermal vasculature is made up of two plexuses.

Vasculature of the skin
instruction: Select Continue to open the remaining text.

_next.ariaLabel: Select here to move to the next.

_items.body: The first is the superficial plexus or subpapillary plexus which is made up of venules that converge where the papillary dermis meets the reticular dermis. The capillaries, end arterioles and venules of the superficial plexus supply the dermal papillae.

The second is the lower or deep plexus, found where the dermis meets the subcutaneous fat of the hypodermis. This deeper plexus is supplied by larger blood vessels. These 2 plexuses are connected to each other by communicating vessels.

Blood flow within the skin fluctuates in response to changes in temperature and control from the nervous system. When the skin is exposed to too much heat, vasodilation occurs which increases the skin blood flow and so dissipates the heat. When the skin is exposed to cold temperatures there is vasoconstriction which decreases the blood flow and so prevents heat loss. This control of blood flow is an essential component of thermoregulation.

title: Innervation – The Supply of Nervous Energy or of Nerve Stimulation to the Skin
body:
The skin is essential in sensory perception, so it contains numerous specialised structures that detect various stimuli. These structures are located in the epidermis and dermis.

Merkel cells or discs are found in the epidermis; these detect light touch. Free nerve endings, which are unmyelinated, detect pain and are also found in the epidermis and can extend into the papillary dermis. These nerve endings can also detect changes in temperature and pressure.

title: Innervation
instruction: Select Continue to open the remaining text.

_next.ariaLabel: Select here to move to the next.

_items.body: Within the dermal papillae are Meissner corpuscles, which mediate touch by detecting changes in texture. These corpuscles are found in greater numbers on the ventral sides of the hands and feet, and particularly on the fingertips.
Deeper within the dermis, and even possibly into the hypodermis, are the Pacini corpuscles with detect pressure and vibrations.

Other specialised structures in the dermis include Krause bulbs which detect cold and Ruffini corpuscles which detect heat. There are also receptors in the hair follicles which detect changes in the position of the hair strands.
All these structures, known as sensory receptors, allow for the skin to feel pain, heat, cold, pressure and proprioception.
A specific area of the skin will be supplied by a single spinal nerve or segment of the spinal cord and is called a dermatome. Adjacent dermatomes may overlap.

title: Skin Physiology
body: The skin and its accessory structures perform several essential functions.
instruction: Select the headings to reveal more information.

_items.body:
The skin is the first physical barrier of protection for the body.

  • It protects the body from the basic elements such as wind and UV radiation but also prevents the invasion of the body by foreign materials and pathogens.
  • The sweat glands produce dermcidin, which has antibacterial properties to further protect the skin.
  • The layers of keratin and glycolipids help to prevent the loss of water from the skin and prevent dehydration.

The specialised nerve endings and structures within the epidermis, dermis and hypodermis allow for the skin to act as a sensory organ.

  • There are different structures, such as Meissner corpuscles and Pacinian corpuscles which respond to different sensory stimuli.
  • The hairs covering the skin also provide sensory input when disturbed.
  • There are pain and temperature receptors throughout the skin and motor nerves which innervate the smooth muscles and control the arrector pili muscles as well as the glands in the skin.
  • All the functions work together to allow the body to interact with and interpret the surrounding environment.

The sympathetic nervous system is continuously monitoring the body’s temperature and adjusting, as necessary.

  • These adjustments are the activation of the sweat glands to produce sweat, which then evaporates from the skin and cools the body through dissipation of the heat.
  • The body can become excessively warm due to exposure to high temperatures or through exertion such as exercise.
  • The arterioles in the dermis will dilate which will also allow for excess heat to be dissipated through the skin.
    • This explains the red “flushed” appearance of the skin that some people experience when they are hot or exercising.
  • When the body becomes too cold the arterioles in the dermis constrict to minimise heat loss.
    • This reduction in circulation can cause the skin to appear more white than normal.
    • The skin may also feel cold to the touch, but the prevention of heat loss means that the internal organs remain warm.

Vitamin D is essential for the normal absorption of calcium and phosphorus in the body.

  • These minerals are very important for healthy bones.
  • The epidermis synthesises vitamin D when it is exposed to UV radiation from the sun.
  • When the skin is exposed to sunlight, a derivative of the steroid cholesterol is converted to cholecalciferol in the skin.
  • This cholecalciferol is then converted to calcidol in the kidneys.
  • The kidneys then convert this compound into calcitriol, which is the active chemical form of vitamin D.
  • In addition to vitamin D’s role in bone health it also plays a role in general immunity against infection from bacteria, viruses or fungi.

title: Nervous Tissue
body:
On a microscopic level the nervous system is made up of two basic types of cells. The two types of cells are:
  • Glial/ neuroglial cells
  • Neurons

title: Neuroglia
body: Neuroglia
instruction: Drag the circle along the horizontal line to reveal more information.

_items.title: Item 1
_items.body: The glial cells, neuroglia or simply glia are a framework of supporting cells that hold all neurons together.

_items.title: Item 2
_items.body: The neuroglia also assist neurons in completing their communication functions.

_items.title: Item 3
_items.body: The glia are found in the brain, spinal cord and the special sense nerves.

title: Neurons
body:
Neurons are an essential component of nervous tissue. Neurons are responsible for communication of electrical stimuli and the corresponding reaction in response to the stimuli.

All neurons have a similar structure.

_items.body: Soma: This is the cell body. The soma contains the nucleus, mitochondria and surrounding cytoplasm. Processes, an extension of the cell, are necessary to the functioning and life of the cell occur within the soma.

_items.body: Axon: An extension from the soma. This is also known as a process. An axon is a thin, single process. It connects the neuron with the target or effector tissue. Neurons have only one axon. The axon may be branched. The axon propagates the signal, which is communicated to one or more cells.

_items.body:
Dendrite: Extensions from the soma. There may be multiple dendrites/ processes emanating from one neuron.

Dendrites receive information from other neurons at the synapses.

Dendrites are usually highly branched processes, providing locations for other neurons to communicate with the cell body.

_items.body: Axon hillock: Structure where axon emerges from the cell body. It is a tapering of the cell body toward the axon fibre. Within the axon hillock the cytoplasm changes to a solution of limited components. This is called axoplasm.

title: Thermoregulation
body: When looking at nervous tissue there are two distinct regions that can be seen.
instruction: Select the pictures below to reveal more information.

_items.backBody: The first is grey matter. Grey matter is the region where there is a concentration of cell bodies and dendrites.

White matter is the second region and is made up of a concentration of axons.

In a fresh tissue sample grey matter may appear pink or red in colour due to the blood in the tissue.

White tissue will appear white due to the myelinated sheaths of the axons.

This fatty sheath is clearly seen as white in colour.

title: Nerves
body: Neurons may be found in clusters within the central nervous system (CNS) and the peripheral nervous system (PNS).

_items.body: In the PNS, a cluster of cell bodies is referred to as a ganglion.
A bundle of axons within the CNS is referred to as a tract.
If the bundle of axons is in the PNS it is called a nerve. Therefore, a bundle of axons traveling through the peripheral nervous system is a nerve.

body:
Within the nerve each axon is covered by a layer called the endoneurium. These axons are bundled together into groups called fascicles.

Each fascicle is covered by a perineurium. The entire nerve is then covered by a connective tissue layer known as the epineurium. Blood vessels supply the tissue with nourishment.

title: Neurotransmission
body:
For the nervous system to function, neurons must be able to send and receive signals. This is called neurotransmission. This transmission is possible because of the charged cellular membrane that surrounds each neuron and the change in this charge in response to neurotransmitters or environmental stimuli.

To understand this concept, we need to understand the charges associated with the membrane and how they are changed.

title: Electrically active cell membranes
displayTitle: ACTION POTENTIALElectrically active cell membranes
instruction: Read the supporting text below the picture then select the forward arrow to scroll to the next one.
mobileInstruction: Read the supporting text below the picture then select the forward arrow to scroll to the next one.
_comment: setCompletionOn = inview | allItems

_items.body:
Most cells in the body use charged particles, ions, to build up a charge across the cell membrane. The cell membrane regulates which substances pass through the membrane and which substances remain on one side only. The cell membrane is a phospholipid bilayer, so substances that can pass directly through the hydrophobic core are able to pass through unassisted. Charged particles are hydrophilic by nature and cannot pass through unaided.

To get these ions across the cell membrane of a neuron, transmembrane proteins are needed, specifically channel proteins. There are also passive transport channels, and active transport pumps which play a role in the generation of action potential.

The ion channels have different configurations – open, closed and inactive. Some ion channels need to be activated in order to open and allow ions to move into and out of the cell. Ion channels are sensitive to their environment and can change their shape accordingly. Voltage-gated channels, which are of importance in action potential, change their structure in response to voltage changes. These channels regulate the relative concentration of ions inside and outside the cell. Normally the inside of the cell is negatively charged. If this charge becomes less negative the channel opens, allowing positively charged ions to move across the membrane and into the cell. The difference in total charge between the inside and the outside of the cell is the membrane potential.

Ions are found in varying concentrations on either side of a membrane and will naturally move from an area of higher concentration to lower concentration. This movement may be into or out of a cell. For ions to be moved against this gradient a protein pump is required. An important pump in the body is the sodium/potassium pump (Na<sup>+</sup>/K<sup>+</sup>) pump.

title: Resting Membrane Protection
instruction: Select Continue to open the remaining text.

_next.ariaLabel: Select here to move to the next.

_items.body: In a neuron (or any other type of cell), at rest, the ion channels are closed, and the ions are distributed across the membrane in a predictable way. The concentration of sodium ions in the extracellular fluid is approximately 10 times that of the concentration inside the neuron. Also, the concentration of potassium ions inside the neuron is approximately 30 times the concentration on the outside.

At rest the neuron is negatively charged, and the charge inside the cell is approximately - 70millivolts more negative than the outside of the cell. This voltage is called the resting membrane potential. This is a steady state and will be maintained until an outside influence, such as a signal from a neighbouring neuron, initiating a change.

title: Action Potential
body: When a neuron is at rest it is in a steady state and without an outside influence this will not change therefore no electrical signal (impulse) will be transmitted from one neuron to the next. For impulse transmission from one neuron to another, the membrane potential needs to change.

_items.body: This process starts with the opening of a sodium channel. This usually occurs when a neurotransmitter binds to receptors on the neuron’s dendrites. The sodium channels in the axon hillock open, and because of the higher concentration of Na<sup>+</sup> outside the cell, there is an influx of sodium takes into the cell down the concentration gradient. Sodium ions carry a positive charge, so the potential within the cell approaches 0. This is known as depolarisation.

Due to the high concentration of sodium ions outside the cell, Na<sup>+</sup> continues to move into the cell after the potential has reached 0 and the potential will become positive. The membrane potential approaches +30 mV, which is called peak potential. The electrical signal (impulse) will be transmitted from one neuron to the next during the peak potential phase.

As the membrane potential approaches +30mV, the potassium channels within the membrane open. Due to the concentration gradient, the potassium ions (K<sup>+</sup>) start to leave the cell and take the positive charge with them. The membrane potential starts to approach 0 again. This is called repolarisation and describes the membrane potential moving back towards the resting potential of -70mV.

Repolarisation returns the membrane potential to its resting value of -70mV, but because the potassium channels are slightly delayed in closing there is a period of hyperpolarisation where the potential overshoots the -70mV and is in fact lower.

instruction: Select Continue to open the remaining text.

_next.ariaLabel: Select here to move to the next.

_items.body: This process above describes the action potential, and this is the electrical signal that nervous tissue uses for communication.

body:
Action potential is what allows for the signal to be transported from one neuron to the next and communication to occur between neurons. The action potential needs to be initiated for the sodium gates to open and the process to begin. The action potential can be initiated by different signals:
  • Neurotransmitter binding to Na+ ligand-gated channel and opening the channel.
  • Mechanically gated Na+ channel opening when physical stimulus affects sensory receptor.
  • Stimulus depolarising Na+ voltage-gated channel (important for action potential).

instruction: Select the pictures below to read more.

_items.backBody: Neurons generate an action potential according to the “all or none” principle. The depolarisation of the cell membrane must reach the threshold of -55mV to trigger the opening of the voltage-gated sodium channel and subsequent events that generate the action potential.

If depolarisation reaches -55mV then the full action potential cycle will occur. This cycle is always the same, no matter how big or strong the stimulus the action potential will always be the same. This is the “all.”

If the stimulus is not strong enough to depolarise the membrane to -55mV threshold, then no action potential will be generated. This is the “none.”
Therefore, either the membrane reaches the threshold, and the cycle occurs as described, or it does not reach the threshold, and nothing happens.

body:
All action potentials have a threshold of -55mV and peak at +30mV. So, no action potential is bigger than another.

Even if the stimulus is stronger, the signal will not be bigger. For example, you will not feel more pain because the stimulus is stronger. The effect of a stronger stimulus is to open more gated channels at the same time but not to increase the strength of the signal.

title: Propagation of Action Potential
body:
Once an action potential has been generated it needs to be moved onto the next neuron for the information to be communicated around the body.

Simply put, the message needs to be moved along the nerve. This is achieved by a process known as propagation. There are two types of propagation which occur.
The first is continuous conduction.
instruction: Select the picture below until you have seen all the information.

_items.body: This is a slower form of propagation and happens in unmyelinated neurons. The action potential is initiated at the axon hillock of the neuron.
There is a concentration of voltage-gated sodium channels at the axon hillock. Rapid depolarisation occurs after the action potential has been initiated.
The Na<sup>+</sup> ions flow into the neuron, and as the ions travel along, they bring a positive charge with them causing more of the membrane to become depolarised.
As the depolarisation spreads more voltage-gated sodium channels are opened allowing the depolarisation to spread even more.

body: The second is saltatory conduction.
instruction: Select the picture below until you have seen all the information.

_items.body: Most nerves in the body are myelinated. The myelin sheath acts as an insulator and alters the way the action potential is propagated through the axon.
Sodium ions enter the axon hillock and spread along the length of the axon. There are no voltage-gated sodium channels until the first node of Ranvier. At this point the axon is exposed.
The action potential is retriggered, and the next segment of axon starts the process again. The action potential “hops” from one node to the next node.
The distances between the nodes are the optimal distance to ensure that the membrane remains depolarised above threshold at the next node. This form of conduction is much faster.

title: Synaptic Transmission
body: Now that a signal has been generated and propagated through the axon of a neuron it needs to be passed onto the next neuron or effector organ for the signal to be communicated across the nervous system.

title: Synaptic Transmission
instruction: Drag the circle along the horizontal line to reveal more information.

_items.title: Item 1
_items.body: The gap between the neurons where the information needs to be transmitted is called the synapse.

_items.title: Item 2
_items.body:
The synapse will typically form between the axon terminals of one neuron and the dendrites of another. However, you do also get axon-to-axon, dendrite-to-dendrite and axon-to-cell body synapses.
  • The neuron transmitting the signal – presynaptic neuron.
  • The neuron receiving the signal – postsynaptic neuron.

_items.title: Item 3
_items.body:
There are two types of synapses which facilitate the transmission of the signal.
  • Chemical synapse – chemical signal released.
  • Electrical synapse – direct connection between two cells.

title: Chemical Synapse
body: The most common synapse is the chemical synapse. The synaptic knob of the axon terminal contains multiple small vesicles, called synaptic vesicles. These vesicles are filled with neurotransmitters.
instruction: Select Continue to open the remaining text.

_next.ariaLabel: Select here to move to the next.

_items.body:
As the action potential reaches the axon terminal the membrane is depolarised, and voltage-gated sodium channels are opened. This depolarisation also causes voltage-gated calcium (Ca2+) channels to open.
The calcium ions that enter the cell cause the synaptic vesicles to bind to the presynaptic membrane. This allows for the neurotransmitters to be released into the synaptic cleft.

The neurotransmitters diffuse across the cleft and join to the receptors on the postsynaptic membrane (neuron or effector organ).
The binding of the neurotransmitters to specific receptors on the postsynaptic membrane causes ligand-gated channels to open.

The neurotransmitters will activate the receptors, and if sufficient receptors are activated a new action potential is generated and the signal is continued down the line. This has an excitatory effect on the postsynaptic neuron.
Neurotransmitters can also have an inhibitory effect on the postsynaptic neuron in which a new action potential is not generated

title: Electrical Synapse
body:
Electrical synapses are less common than chemical synapses. In an electrical synapse the presynaptic and postsynaptic neurons are very close together and connected by channel proteins, known as gap junctions.

These gap junctions allow the signal to be transmitted directly from one cell to the next. Transmission across these synapses is almost instantaneous, making them very important in things such as a reflex action.

title: Control of Neurotransmission
body: Once neurotransmission has occurred, the neurotransmitter must be cleared from the synaptic cleft. This allows the postsynaptic membrane to “reset” and prepare for the next signal.
instruction: Select the picture below to read more.

_items.backBody:
There are three ways in which the neurotransmitter can be cleared:
  • Diffuse away from the synaptic cleft
  • Degradation by enzymes in the synaptic cleft
  • Recycled by presynaptic neuron
The neuron is now ready to receive the next signal and continue neurotransmission.

title: Pain
body: Pain is defined as a sensation of discomfort, distress or agony, resulting from the stimulation of specialised nerve endings.
instruction: Select the picture below until you have read all of the information.

_items.body: Pain signals actual or potential injury to the body.
Pain serves as a protective mechanism insofar as it warns the sufferer that there is tissue damage and induces the sufferer to withdraw or remove from the source.
Pain is not only a sensation or physical awareness of discomfort but also includes the perception and subjective interpretation of pain.
Perception provides information as to the location and intensity of the pain.
There is also an emotional response associated with pain, which can affect the perception of pain.

title: Sensory System
body:
The sensory system is a part of the nervous system responsible for processing sensory information.

The sensory system responds to information from the external environment as well as the internal environment of our bodies. The stimuli that are received from varying sources and of different types, are converted into electrochemical signals in the nervous system. The stimulus causes the receptor to produce an action potential, which is relayed to the CNS, interpreted and the appropriate response generated.

It is important to make the distinction between sensation and perception.

instruction: Select the pictures below to read more.

_items.backBody: Sensation is the activation of sensory receptors at the level of stimulus.
Perception is the central processing of sensory stimuli into a meaningful pattern.

body: Perception is dependent on sensation. However, not all sensations are perceived by the brain.

title: Sensory receptors
body:
Sensory receptors, within the peripheral nervous system, are activated by stimuli from the environment. Different stimuli will activate different sensory receptors.

These receptors are classified structurally and functionally.

Structural classification is based on the cell type and position in relation to the stimuli whilst functional classification is how the stimulus changes the cell membrane potential (transduction).

Functional Receptors
ChemoreceptorsInterpret chemical stimuli, such as the taste or smell.
OsmoreceptorsInterpret changes to solute concentrations in the body.
MechanoreceptorsInterpret mechanical changes caused by pressure or distortion.

title: Sensory pathways
instruction: Read the supporting text below the picture then select the forward arrow to scroll to the next one.
mobileInstruction: Read the supporting text below the picture then select the forward arrow to scroll to the next one.
_comment: setCompletionOn = inview | allItems

_items.body:
Once the stimulus has been sensed by the receptors it needs to be transmitted to the CNS for perception.

A sensory pathway carries the signal to the CNS, for the CNS to coordinate the correct sensory input with the correct motor output of the peripheral nerves.

The parts of the CNS that are involved with this process are:
  • Spinal cord
  • Brain stem
  • Diencephalon
  • Cerebral cortex
  • Subcortical structures

The sensory pathway that carries information from the peripheral nerves to the brain is referred to as the ascending pathway.

The ascending pathways are:
  • Dorsal column system – information from below the neck to the brain
  • Spinothalamic tract – information from below the neck to the brain
  • Trigeminal pathway – information from the face, mouth, nasal cavity and head to the brain

title: Perception in the Brain
body: The parts of the brain involved with perception of sensory inputs are the diencephalon and the cerebral cortex.
instruction: Select the button below the text to see more.

_next.ariaLabel: Select here to move to the next.

_items.body:
The diencephalon, involving the hypothalamus and thalamus, is an important relay for information between the cerebrum and the rest of the nervous system.

The hypothalamus plays a role in both the somatic and autonomic nervous systems. The hypothalamus is also connected to the limbic system which controls emotions and memories.

Information enters the thalamus through the special senses and somatosensory tracts, with each sensory system relayed through a specific nucleus in the thalamus.

The thalamus is the central point for the transfer of information to the cerebral cortex where conscious sensory perception occurs. The only exception to this is the sense of smell, which goes directly to the limbic system and hypothalamus.

The cerebral cortex is responsible for the cortical processing of information.

There are specific regions within the cerebral cortex where specific information is relayed. These regions are described as the somatosensory cortex, gustatory cortex, visual cortex etc., depending on the sense associated with the particular cortex.

We however do not experience these senses in pieces but rather as a seamless sensory experience, combining the different senses into a full experience.

title: Nociceptors
body:
Nociceptors are responsible for detecting pain. Pain is also known as nociception. Nociception occurs due to stimuli that the body perceives to be a threat or injurious.

Nociceptors are free nerve endings that act as high-threshold mechanoreceptors. These receptors can respond to an actual injury such as burning the skin or a perceived threat that is in fact a harmless stimulus.

_items.body: Nociceptors are free nerve endings that function as high-threshold mechanoreceptors.
Many pain receptors are specialised chemoreceptors and respond to substances such as bradykinins, substance P and histamines.
These substances induce a noxious reaction which the body responds to as pain.
Most axons are slow conducting, only lightly myelinated A-delta fibres and detect the well localised initial pain associated with an injury or pricking cutaneous pain.
There are unmyelinated C nerve fibres which conduct deeper and slower pain, known as secondary pain. This pain is more persistent and may be felt as burning pain.
These unmyelinated C nerve fibres also detect deep pain in the viscera, muscles and joints.

title: Pain Perception
body: Pain is a part of the sensation of touch. Pain serves the purposes of informing the brain to sensations but also to protect the body from potential damage. Pain can also have an emotional aspect attached to it. This makes perception of pain a complex process.
instruction: Select the button below until you have opened all the points.

_next.ariaLabel: Select here to move to the next.

_items.body: Most situations that are dangerous to the body, external and internal, are painful. This allows the body to identify and respond to noxious stimuli. Noxious stimuli are stimuli that create tissue damage and activate nociceptors.

Nociceptors respond to damage to tissues or the threat of damage to tissues. They also respond to chemical substances released from tissue that is damaged. Nociceptors are free nerve endings located in the skin, viscera, muscles and joints. Nociceptors contain ion channels known as transient receptor potential (TRP) channels. These channels act like potassium gated channels, and open in response to pain signals. Noxious stimuli generate an action potential, which is transported to the spinal cord and brain.

The pathways used to transport pain signals are the dorsal root column and spinothalamic tract. If the stimulus is generated in the tissues of the head and face the signals will move through the trigeminal pathway. There are no nociceptors located in the CNS itself.

body:
Nociceptors do not all have the same sensitivity. The sensitivity will depend on the receptors’ response to mechanical, thermal or chemical stimuli that occurs when there is an injury or damage to the tissue.

There are four types of skin nociceptors:

title: Types of Nociceptors

_items.title: High threshold mechanoreceptors/ nociceptive specific neurons
_items.body: Respond to intense mechanical stimuli such as cutting, pinching and stretching

_items.title: Thermal nociceptors
_items.body: Respond to intense chemical stimuli and to changes in temperature

_items.title: Chemical nociceptors
_items.body: Respond only to chemical stimuli or thermal noxious stimuli

_items.title: Polymodal nociceptors
_items.body: Respond to a variety of noxious and non-noxious high intensity mechanical, chemical and thermal stimuli

instruction: Select the pictures below to read more.

_items.backBody:
Joint capsules and ligaments contain three types of nociceptors:
  • High threshold mechanoreceptors
  • Polymodal nociceptors
  • “Silent” nociceptors
Many of the nerve fibres whose endings are found in the joint capsules and ligaments also release neuropeptides, which contribute to inflammation of the joints and ligaments.

Visceral organs contain the following nociceptors:
  • Mechanoreceptors
  • Thermal receptors
  • Chemical receptors
  • “Silent” receptors
These nociceptors are found throughout the visceral organs of the body, with some areas more densely populated than others. The pathway that signals from visceral receptors travel along is different from the pathway used by signals from the skin receptors.

body:
Silent nociceptors, also known as sleep nociceptors, are found in the skin and deep tissues. These receptors do not respond to normal noxious mechanical stimuli. Rather they respond to the mechanical stimulation associated with inflammation and tissue damage.

The activation of these nociceptors may lead to hyperalgesia, central sensitisation or allodynia. Many visceral nociceptors are silent nociceptors.

title: Pain Fibres
body:
There are different types of axons associated with the neurons and receptors that feel pain. Two types of fibres that are found are A-delta fibres and C fibres.

The fibres are differentiated based on whether they are myelinated, their thickness and the speed at which they can conduct signals. The speed at which the fibres conduct signals is directly related to the diameter of the fibre and whether it is myelinated or not.
instruction: Select Continue to open the remaining text.

_next.ariaLabel: Select here to move to the next.

_items.body:
A-delta fibres are myelinated fibres with a diameter of 2 – 5 mm. These fibres conduct signals at a speed of 5 – 40m/sec. This is faster than C fibres. A-delta fibres mainly carry signals from mechanoreceptors and mechano-thermal receptors.

These fibres are found in fewer areas across the body and because of this they give a precise location of pain. These fibres sense what is described as “fast” pain.

C fibres are unmyelinated with a diameter of 0.4 – 1.2 mm. These fibres conduct signals at a speed of 0.5 – 2 m/sec. Therefore, they are slower than A-delta fibres. C fibres carry signals from high intensity mechanoreceptors, thermal receptors and chemical receptors. They also carry information from polymodal receptors.

C fibres are more commonly found than A-delta fibres (approximately 70% of fibres are C fibres). Due to the wider distribution of these fibres, they give less precise localisation of pain. These fibres sense what is described as “slow” pain. Free nerve endings have both A-delta and C fibres.

title: Nocineurons
instruction: Select the picture below until you have seen all the information.

_items.body: The nociceptors that have been discussed so far are those found in the peripheral nervous system. There are nociceptors located in the spinal cord, known as nocineurons.
Nocineurons are activated by substances released by the axon terminals that synapse with the dorsal root ganglion. The released substances include substance P, glutamate and aspartate to name a few.
This leads to centralised sensitisation.

body:
There are four types of nocineurons in the spinal cord.

High threshold mechanoreceptors / nociceptive specific neuronsExcited by noxious cutaneous or visceral stimuli. The nociceptive fibres release glutamate and neuropeptides which excite dorsal horn neurons.
Chemical nociceptor neuronsExcited by chemical or thermal noxious stimuli in the skin or viscera.
Thermal nociceptor neuronsExcited by chemical or thermal noxious stimuli in the skin or viscera.
Polymodal nociceptor neurons/multi or wide dynamic range nociceptive neuronsExcited by noxious and non-noxious cutaneous and / or visceral stimuli and respond to mechanical, chemical and thermal stimuli. Degree of response is related to intensity of stimuli.

title: Types of Pain
body: There are various ways to classify pain. The types of pain can be classified by cause and described as nociceptive or neuropathic.

instruction: Select each picture to learn more.

_items.backBody:
• Caused by injury to body tissue.
  • Stimulation of nociceptors.
  • Most pain, particularly acute pain, is nociceptive.
  • Includes pain caused by inflammation.
  • Two types:
    • Somatic pain.
    • Visceral pain.

• Dysfunction or damage to central or peripheral nervous system:
    • Brain or spinal cord.
    • Peripheral nerves.
  • Caused by:
    • Pressure on a specific nerve.
    • Nerve damage due to disease such as diabetes mellitus.
    • CNS does not properly transmit/interpret pain signals.

title: Types of Pain
body: These pain categories can then be further divided.
instruction: Select the tab below to learn more.

_items.title: Somatic Pain
_items.body:
• Activation of receptors located in:
    • Skin, subcutaneous tissues, fascia, connective tissues, bones and joint capsules.
  • Activation of receptors leads to sharp or dull localised pain.
  • May be associated with burning.

_items.title: Visceral Pain
_items.body:
• Activation of nociceptors in viscera and surrounding connective tissue.
  • Obstruction of hollow organ will produce poorly localised, deep and possibly cramping pain.
  • This pain may be referred to remote sites.
  • Pain due to injury to viscera will produce more localised and sharp pain.

title: Acute Pain
body:
Acute pain is short lived and intense pain. This type of pain is usually associated with an injury and is because of activation of the peripheral pain receptors and their specific C-fibres and A-delta fibres (nociceptors).

Acute pain has a sudden onset and is limited, lasting days or weeks. Severe acute pain can cause anxiety, tachycardia, increased respiratory rate, elevated blood pressure, sweating and dilated pupils. These symptoms are caused by hyperactivity of the sympathetic nervous system.

title: Chronic Pain
body:
Chronic pain is a persistent and on-going pain and is often an indication of a long-term illness or injury. Chronic pain related to tissue injury is due to nerve fibres that are continually activated causing the consistent sensation of pain. The severity of the injury is not always an indication of pain severity, and chronic pain can occur in the absence of tissue damage.

Chronic pain can be secondary to an underlying disease such as cancer or primary, that is caused by the disease itself. Chronic pain can also develop if there is ongoing damage to or dysfunction of the peripheral or central nervous systems. This leads to neuropathic pain. Chronic pain is defined as lasting or recurring for longer than 3 – 6 months.

Chronic pain usually doesn’t involve activation of the sympathetic nervous system, but patients may experience additional comorbidities such as disturbed sleep, depression and decreased energy.

title: Chemical Mediators of Pain
body: When tissue is damaged there are chemical mediators which are released. These mediators will contribute to the activation of nociceptors and the feeling of pain. Some of these mediators activate TRP channels and initiate action potentials.
instruction: Select the picture below until you have seen all the information.

_items.body: When tissue is damaged or injured, mediators are released from the lysed cells as well as additional substances being recruited to the injury site.

The release of these substances sensitises nociceptors and reduces their threshold. This is called peripheral sensitisation. This is soon followed by vasodilation of the area and inflammation. This area will now have a lowered pain threshold.
This process is due to the chemical mediators released after tissue damage. Chemical mediators include histamine, serotonin, globulin and protein kinases.

title: Introduction
body:
Anaesthesia is the use of medications (anaesthetics) to prevent sensations of pain during procedures or surgery. Anaesthetics temporarily block sensory signals from travelling between the site of pain and the brain.

Anaesthetics can be used to numb a specific area of the body (local or regional anaesthesia) and cause unconsciousness so that more invasive surgery can be carried out (general anaesthesia).

title: Topical Anaesthesia
body:
Topical anaesthesia is defined as the superficial loss of sensation in conjunctiva, mucous membranes or skin produced by the direct application of local anaesthetic solutions, ointments, gels or sprays. It allows for anaesthesia without the use of injections and the associated needle anxiety and tissue oedema.

Topical anaesthesia is widely used in various medical procedures including ophthalmology, dentistry and aesthetic surgery.
Topical anaesthetic works at the site where it is applied by reversibly blocking the nerve conduction of the nerves in the area. This produces a temporary loss of sensation in the area.

This decreased permeability prevents depolarization from occurring and generation of the action potential which in turn prevents conduction of nerve signals.

_items.body: Topical anaesthetics are better able to penetrate mucosal surfaces such as those in the mouth and genitals because there is no keratinised surface i.e. no stratum corneum.

There are three ways in which the anaesthetic can cross the stratum corneum:
  • Intracellular route – through the spaces between the cornified keratinocytes.
  • Para or transcellular route – through the cornified keratinocytes.
  • Trans appendageal route (shunt pathway) – through the openings of the hair follicles and sweat glands.

body:
The delivery of an anaesthetic agent is impacted by several factors.

These include:
instruction: Select the pictures below to read more.

_items.backBody: Drug form – free bases penetrate the stratum corneum better than the salt form, which will require a specialised delivery method.

Melting point and eutectic mixtures – the lower the melting point, the better the penetration. A eutectic mixture has a lower melting point than either component on its own, which improves penetration.
Drug concentration – a higher concentration of drug relates to a higher rate of penetration.
Skin permeation enhancers – compounds which increase skin permeability, temporarily and reversibly.

title: Local Anaesthetic Agents
body:
Local anaesthetics provide a reversible loss of sensation and reduce pain to facilitate surgical procedures. Local anaesthetic agents are used for topical anaesthesia. These local anaesthetics are weak bases and are made up of three important structures:
  • Aromatic ring
  • Intermediate ester or amide chain
  • Tertiary amine

_graphic.attribution: Basic chemical structure of local anaesthetic agents

instruction: Select the pictures below to read more.

_items.backBody:
The aromatic ring is lipophilic, which means it has an affinity for lipids. The aromatic ring is responsible for lipid solubility and allows the agent to pass through the cell membrane and myelin sheath of the nerves.

The cell membrane and myelin sheath are composed of lipids. This means that local anaesthetic can move into the cell membrane and bind to the sodium channels and thereby inhibit depolarisation and nerve conduction.

The terminal amine is hydrophilic. It can exist in two forms. The first is in a tertiary form which makes the molecule lipid soluble, but not water soluble. In the quaternary form the molecule carries a positive charge which makes it water soluble.

The intermediate chain determines if the local anaesthetic belongs to the amino ester or amino amide group. Each group has a specific set of properties and characteristics.

body: The intermediate chain determines if the local anaesthetic belongs to the amino ester or amino amide group. Each group has a specific set of properties and characteristics.

_items.body: Ester-linked local anaesthetics are hydrolysed by esterases found in plasma. These esterases are called pseudocholinesterases.
Pseudocholinesterase is an enzyme present in the blood and in certain organs that hydrolyses acetylcholine more slowly than acetylcholinesterase.
Another characteristic of amino ester local anaesthetic is that hydrolysis of this agent leads to the formation of the by-product para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA).
It is this molecule which leads to the allergic reactions more commonly seen with this group of local anaesthetics than with the amino amide anaesthetic agents.

instruction: Select the tabs below to learn more.

_items.body:
Cocaine was the first local anaesthetic to be discovered. It was discovered in 1860 and is naturally found in the leaves of cocoa shrub.

Cocaine blocks nerve conduction as well as causing vasoconstriction and inhibition of norepinephrine uptake. The inhibition of norepinephrine uptake leads to stimulation of the central nervous system.

Cocaine also inhibits the uptake of dopamine. It is these properties that generate the euphoric state experienced with cocaine.
Procaine was the first synthetically made local anaesthetic. Procaine has a low potency, slow onset of action and short duration of action.

Tetracaine was introduced in 1932. It is a long-acting amino ester and more potent than procaine. It is also more slowly metabolised than other local anaesthetics, which can make it more toxic.

Tetracaine is used in various topical applications or in spinal anaesthesia when a long-acting agent is required.

title: Lidocaine
body:
Lidocaine is one of the most common amino amide local anaesthetics and was first discovered in 1948. Lidocaine is rapidly absorbed through the gastrointestinal tract, when injected or when inhaled making it a versatile agent. Lidocaine can also be used in topical formulation. Lidocaine may also be known as lignocaine.

90% of lidocaine is metabolised in the liver with the majority being excreted in the urine.

Adverse effects may be due to systemic toxicity and can affect the cardiovascular and central nervous systems.

title: Prilocaine
body: Prilocaine has a pharmacological profile similar to that of lidocaine with an intermediate duration of action. Prilocaine differs from lidocaine in that it does not cause vasodilation and it has a greater volume of distribution.
instruction: Select the pictures below to read more.

_items.backBody: The distribution means that prilocaine has a lower risk of toxicity when compared to lidocaine. The disadvantage of prilocaine is its tendency to cause methemoglobinemia.
Methaemoglobinemia (MetHb) is a blood disorder characterised by an abnormal amount of methaemoglobin being produced. Methaemoglobin is a form of haemoglobin.
Haemoglobin is the protein found in red blood cells which is responsible for the transportation of oxygen around the body.

body:
Methemoglobinemia can be inherited or acquired. There are two forms of inherited MetHb.

Type 1 occurs when the patient inherits a gene from both parents and the red blood cells lack the enzyme called cytochrome b5 reductase.

Type 2 is caused by a defect in the haemoglobin protein itself. Only one parent needs to pass the gene onto the child. This disease is also called haemoglobin M disease. The acquired form is more common and occurs after exposure to certain anaesthetics, antibiotics, nitrobenzene or nitrites.

Patients with acquired methemoglobinemia will have a bluish colour to their skin due to lack of oxygen (cyanosis), will experience headaches, fatigue, and shortness of breath and lack of energy. Mild cases of acquired MetHb may not require treatment. Severe acquired MetHb is treated with IV administration of methylene blue.

title: Topical Anaesthesia Toxicity
body: Although generally safe, local anaesthetics can be toxic if administered inappropriately. Adverse effects are usually due to high plasma concentrations of the agent. This can occur from excessive dose, delayed drug clearance and administration to vascular tissue.

title: EMLA Overview
body:
EMLA (eutectic mixture of local anaesthetics) is available as a cream and a patch. The EMLA emulsion is an oil-in-water emulsion system in which the oil phase consists of a eutectic mixture of the base forms of lidocaine and prilocaine in a 1:1 ratio.

A eutectic mixture is defined as a mixture of two or more substances that usually do not interact to form a new chemical compound but, at certain ratios, inhibit the crystallisation process of one another and so form a new compound with a lower melting point than any of the individual components.

_graphic.attribution: EMLA applied in a thick layer to intact skin

title: Mechanism of Action
body:
EMLA is a eutectic mixture of lidocaine and prilocaine in an oil-in-water emulsion.

The eutectic mixtures means that the crystalline bases of lidocaine and prilocaine mix to create a lower melting point than would be achieved individually, which creates the ideal circumstances for skin penetration.

Lidocaine and prilocaine are mixed at a 1:1 ratio. The melting point of EMLA is therefore lower than that of lidocaine and prilocaine alone.

Looking at the graph below the eutectic melting point is labelled “e”. Below this melting point both lidocaine and prilocaine will be solids but if the temperature rises above the eutectic melting point, then both compounds will become liquid.
instruction: Select Continue to open the remaining text.

_next.ariaLabel: Select here to move to the next.

_items.body: The melting point of lidocaine is 67 °C and prilocaine is 37 °C. When these 2 compounds are combined to form EMLA the melting point becomes 18 °C.

When EMLA is applied to skin as room temperature the mixture melts because the temperature is higher than the melting point, and the EMLA becomes liquid on the skin. These characteristics allow for an effective and convenient local topical anaesthetic to be formulated.

Polyoxyetheylene hydrogenated castor oil surfactant is added to the 1:1 eutectic mixture of lidocaine and prilocaine during the formation of EMLA cream.

This surfactant changes the intermolecular interactions between the drugs in the aqueous (liquid) phase to form both nanoparticles and large oil droplets. The nanoparticles are able to penetrate the skin and rapidly diffuse through unbroken skin.

body: The large oil droplets act as reservoirs in which the drug is stored. EMLA has a penetration efficacy 5X that of a eutectic oil alone.

title: Indications
body: EMLA is available as a cream and a patch, with a wide variety of indications.
instruction: Select the pictures below to read more.

_items.backBody:
The cream can be used for:
  • Topical anaesthesia of the skin in connection with:
    • Needle insertion (e.g., IV catheters or blood sampling).
    • Superficial surgical procedures.
  • Topical anaesthesia of genital mucosa (in adults and children older than 12 years):
    • Prior to superficial surgical procedures.
    • Prior to infiltration anaesthesia.
  • Topical anaesthesia of leg ulcers (in adults only):
    • Facilitate cleansing or debridement.

The patch can be used for:
  • Topical anaesthesia of intact skin
    • Minor procedures such as needle insertion
    • Surgical treatment of localised lesions

body:
Overall EMLA can be used in a wide variety of settings, by numerous types of health care professionals and to provide anaesthesia and pain reduction in a range of procedures.

There is a large database of efficacy demonstrating the proven use of EMLA. EMLA is easy to apply and can be used at home if required prior to procedures done by a health care professional.

title: EMLA Cream and Patch
body:
EMLA is available as a cream and a patch. There are various settings in which one may be more appropriate than another, however the patch is as effective as the cream.

An EMLA patch provides several benefits with regards to ease of use including:
instruction: Select Continue to open the remaining text.

_next.ariaLabel: Select here to move to the next.

_items.body:
• Single unit dosage
  • Simplifies and speeds up the application of EMLA
  • Allows for control of the dose administered per application
  • Prevents under or over dosage

• Easy to apply, not messy, no additional dressing necessary
  • Limited patient or parental instruction required
  • Particularly appropriate in the outpatient setting or before bringing patients in for in-patient procedures

body: The waiting time required when applying EMLA cream can be used advantageously:
instruction: Select each checkmark on the picture to read more.
mobileInstruction: Select each checkmark to read more.
_comment: setCompletionOn = inview | allItems

_items.body:
• Can be used effectively for outpatients without changing routine practices or wasting time.
  • Children can continue with activities while waiting for EMLA to penetrate skin.
  • Children can be counselled to reduced anticipatory anxiety and fear e.g., a “magic cream” is being used to take away the pain.
_items._comment: Supported classes = 'hide-desktop-image' | 'hide-popup-image'. Additional classes can be used but they must be predefined in one of the Less files

body: Although EMLA is generally reported as non-toxic after infancy, local adverse effects are possible:

_items.text: Seizures and respiratory depression (1 reported case)
Methaemoglobinaemia (most dangerous and potentially fatal complication reported in neonates)

body:
In children/neonates younger than 3 months a transient, clinically insignificant increase in methaemoglobin level is commonly observed up to 12 hours after an application of EMLA.

Patients with defective glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase or congenital or idiopathic methaemoglobinaemia are more susceptible to drug-induced methaemoglobinaemia.

Until further clinical data are available, EMLA should not be used in the following cases:
  • In infants between 0 to 12 months of age receiving treatment with methaemoglobin-inducing agents.
  • In preterm infants with a gestational age less than 37 weeks (cream).

body:
EMLA can be used to reduce pain associated with vaccinations. Vaccinations are a common yet painful needle procedure worldwide.

Some patients develop a high level of fear of needles and subsequent needle procedures can induce significant distress in the patient. Children are often concerned about the pain and require an intervention for pain at a lower level of pain intensity than an adult would.

title: Vaccinations
instruction: Select the checkmark on the picture to read more.
mobileInstruction: Select each checkmark to read more.
_comment: setCompletionOn = inview | allItems

_items.body: The World Health Organisation (WHO) considers pain mitigation part of good vaccination clinical practice. In addition, the Help Eliminate Pain in Kids (HELPinKIDS) 2010 vaccination guidelines state that topical anaesthesia is strongly recommended before vaccination injections in children younger than 12 years of age.
_items._comment: Supported classes = 'hide-desktop-image' | 'hide-popup-image'. Additional classes can be used but they must be predefined in one of the Less files

body:
Infants and children have many vaccinations throughout their lives. On average in the first 6 years of a child’s life they will have more than 20 vaccinations, and from 7 to 18 years they can have 10 or more vaccinations.

Long after the acutely painful sensation is gone, the emotional sequelae surrounding the experience can linger. Over time, unmitigated pain may increase fear, which in turn, may increase pain at future procedures.
There are certain consequences of pain and anxiety associated with vaccinations.
instruction: Select the tabs below to learn more.
_comment: setCompletionOn = inview | allItems

_items.title: Vaccine hesitancy and compromised immunity
_items.body: Herd immunity can be compromised which could lead to outbreaks of vaccine-preventable illnesses.

_items.title: Escalating pain
_items.body:
• Many patients receive more than one vaccination in a single visit
  • Some vaccinations are inherently more painful than others
  • Pain can escalate with subsequent vaccinations

_items.title: Preference of children
_items.body:
• Majority of children are afraid of needles and prefer analgesics to be used
  • Topical anaesthetics are recommended in guidelines, particularly for infants

body: Guidelines recommend the use of topical anaesthetics to reduce pain associated with vaccinations. The rationale behind these recommendations includes:
instruction: Select Continue to open the remaining text.

_next.ariaLabel: Select here to move to the next.

_items.body: Having a well-established profile and are an established therapy for needle-related pain mitigation in patients of all ages.
Shown to reduce acute distress.
Improve adherence to immunisation schedule, and having no adverse effect on the immune response.

body: The use of topical anaesthetics requires additional time. This waiting can be incorporated into the clinic wait time prior to vaccinations or used at home before coming to the clinic.

title: Cosmetology
body: Botox is the injection of the toxin produced by the bacterium Clostridium botulinum into the muscles of the face to paralyse the muscles and therefore treat wrinkles and fine lines.

title: Botox
body: Botox requires multiple percutaneous injections to be done on the forehead and around the eyes, depending on the type of procedure.
instruction: Select each checkmark on the picture to read more.
mobileInstruction: Select each checkmark to read more.
_comment: setCompletionOn = inview | allItems

_items.body:
• Although Botox is a relatively simple and fast-acting procedure it is associated with pain and anxiety. Injections in and around the face can provoke more sensitivity and anxiety than other areas of the body.
  • Therefore, some patients may refuse to have repeated injections due to the pain. Topical anaesthetic creams can be used to minimise the pain during the procedure.
_items._comment: Supported classes = 'hide-desktop-image' | 'hide-popup-image'. Additional classes can be used but they must be predefined in one of the Less files

body: A study by Eppley et al showed EMLA to reduce pain sensation by 60% that it was effective in improving the discomfort of Botox injections, was easy and convenient to use and was more effective in pain control than other topical anaesthetics, for example ice. Occlusive dressing was also not necessary.

title: Epilation
body:
Epilation involves electrolysis and diathermy, both of which are described by patients as unpleasant or painful. Infiltration of local anaesthetic is also a painful procedure.

EMLA is highly concentrated, diffusible at room temperature and more effective than lidocaine alone.

EMLA therefore provides effective anaesthesia during epilation. Patients also reported less pain after the procedure after using EMLA.

title: Superficial Skin Procedures
body:
EMLA can be used prior to a medium-depth chemical peel. The benefits of using EMLA include:
  • Decreased discomfort during application of chemical peel
  • Decrease in discomfort without influencing clinical or histopathological result
  • No delayed healing or evidence of contact dermatitis

Therefore, EMLA provides a statistically significant decrease in pain both during the initial application of the chemical peel and during frosting and there is a decrease in discomfort after the procedure is completed.
